'''''Salvia involucrata''''', the '''roseleaf sage''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the sage [[family (botany)|family]] [[Lamiaceae]].<ref name="IPNISinvolucrata">{{IPNI|id=456447-1|date=29 January 2009}}</ref> This [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] is native to the [[Mexico|Mexican]] states of [[Puebla]], [[Tamaulipas]], and [[Veracruz]], growing in shady places such as the edge of forests. Its [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''involucrata'' refers to the prominent flower [[bract]]s, which are large and colorful.<ref name="Clebsch">{{cite book|last1=Clebsch|first1=Betsy|last2=Barner|first2=Carol D.|title=The New Book of Salvias|publisher=Timber Press|year=2003|pages=155–158|isbn=978-0-88192-560-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NM0iwB8GrQYC&pg=PA155}}</ref>

==Description==
''Salvia involucrata'' grows {{cvt|5|ft|m|abbr=on}} or taller before it starts blooming in late summer. The plant's flowers and bracts are a reddish, beetroot color. The bracts occur in pairs which envelop three flowers each, falling away as the flowers expand. The plant's leaves are small, flat mid-green, slightly cordate-shaped. Unusually, the leaves' [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s and [[vein]]s share the flowers' beetroot-reddish hue.<ref name="Clebsch"/> Genetically, the species has eleven (11) tetraploidal [[chromosome]]s.<ref name="Alberto2008">{{cite journal|last1=Alberto|first1=Cecilia M.|last2=Sanso|first2=A. Mariel|last3=Xifreda|first3=Cecilia C.|date=2003-03-28|title=Chromosomal studies in species of Salvia (Lamiaceae) from Argentina|journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society|publisher=The Linnean Society of London|location=London, UK|volume=141|issue=4|pages=483–490|doi=10.1046/j.1095-8339.2003.t01-1-00178.x|doi-access=free|hdl=11336/106294|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Salvia involucrata''<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Salvia involucrata''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/16339/Salvia-involucrata/Details | access-date = 17 February 2021}}</ref> and its cultivars 'Bethellii'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Salvia involucrata'' 'Bethellii'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/96630/Salvia-involucrata-Bethellii/Details | access-date = 17 February 2021}}</ref> and 'Boutin'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Salvia involucrata'' 'Boutin'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/60127/Salvia-involucrata-Boutin/Details | access-date = 17 February 2021}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web 
| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 
| page = 94 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 12 October 2018}}</ref> 'Bethellii' was introduced in 1881 for its compact habit and large ovoid leaves. Another cultivar, common in France and Britain, is 'Deschamsiana', which was chosen in 1869 for the bright rose color of its inflated flowers. Cultivars that have found popularity in the U.S. include 'Hidalgo', 'El Butano', and 'El Cielo'—each named after the place in Mexico where it was collected.<ref name="Clebsch"/>

''Salvia involucrata'' breeds freely with other ''[[Salvia]]'' species, resulting in many hybrids at [[University of California Botanical Garden]] that show hybrid vigor. Some of these hybrid plants are known to grow up to six feet high, with a longer blooming period. 'Mulberry Jam', a smaller hybrid with upright growth, stronger stems, and continuous blooming from summer to frost was introduced in 1995 by Betsy Clebsch.<ref name="Clebsch"/>

As a garden plant, it prefers good drainage, half to three-quarter a day of sun, humus enriched soil, and deep watering once a week. Propagation is by division or cuttings, which can be rooted in late summer or early autumn. The plant will grow back from the ground after light freezes. In early spring, it should be pruned back to active nodes a few inches from the crown.<ref name="Clebsch"/>

==In medicine==
Historically, ''S. involucrata'' along with several other members of its genus have been used as a memory-enhancer in traditional [[herbal medicine]]. Scientific studies seeking to verify this have shown that extracts of ''S. involucrata'' (along with other ''Salvia'' species) contained significant amounts of [[cerebral cortex]]-relevant compounds, including with those with binding affinity to [[acetylcholine receptors]].<ref name="Wake2000">{{cite journal|last1=Wake|first1=George|last2=Court|first2=Jennifer|last3=Pickering|first3=Anne|last4=Lewis|first4=Rhiannon|last5=Wilkins|first5=Richard|last6=Perry|first6=Elaine|date=February 2000|title=CNS acetylcholine receptor activity in European medicinal plants traditionally used to improve failing memory |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|publisher=Elsevier Science Ireland Ltd.| location=Ireland|volume=69|issue=2|pages=105–114|doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(99)00113-0|pmid=10687867   }}</ref> The species has also been used at least once in the past as an indicator of [[carbon dioxide]] metabolism. In a 1919 study, ''Salvia involucrata'' was used to determine the effects of [[diethyl ether|ether]] on the rate of CO<sub>2</sub> respiration on dying cells. The study found that petals of ''S. involucrata'' immersed in ether consumed more oxygen as the cells expired.<ref name="Irwin1919">{{cite journal|last=Irwin|first=Marian|date=1919-03-20|title=Increased production of carbon dioxide accompanied by decrease of acidity|journal=The Journal of General Physiology|volume=1|issue=4|pages=399–403|pmid=19871754|pmc=2140318|doi=10.1085/jgp.1.4.399}}</ref>
